headline: mixed
texts: A mixed result. Some of the hernia anatomy and management logic is firm, and some still rests on recall. The sections below show which, and the review order starts with the weakest.
Direct versus indirect is partly there. Anchor one rule: indirect is lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through the deep ring, direct is medial through the posterior wall.
Hesselbach's triangle is shaky. Say the three sides aloud: inferior epigastric artery, lateral rectus border, inguinal ligament. Exam keys use the inguinal ligament, not Cooper's, as the base.
Inguinal versus femoral position is shaky. Fix it: inguinal is above and medial to the pubic tubercle, femoral is below and lateral.
Cause and clinical picture are shaky. Pair them: indirect with patent processus, scrotal descent and lateral reduction; direct with acquired wall weakness and straight-back reduction.

The bedside tests are a gap. Occlusion of the deep ring controls an indirect sac while a direct sac still appears medial. In Zieman's test, index suggests indirect, middle direct, ring finger femoral.
The 'most common' answers are shaky. Remember that indirect inguinal leads overall, in both sexes and in children, even though femoral is relatively commoner in women.
Strangulation risk is shaky. Two rankings: among inguinal hernias indirect strangulates more than direct, but among all groin hernias femoral is highest. Read the scope word.
First step and investigation are shaky. Strangulation signs mean resuscitation and emergency surgery with no forceful taxis. For tests: none if evident, ultrasound for occult, MRI if inconclusive.
Choosing the operation is shaky. Sort by patient: child herniotomy, adult open Lichtenstein, bilateral or recurrent laparoscopic, Shouldice as the best tissue repair. Older keys said Bassini.
Nerves and triangles are shaky. Pair them: ilioinguinal with open repair, lateral femoral cutaneous with laparoscopic repair, doom with vessels, pain with nerves.
The named hernias are shaky. Anchor each: Amyand is appendix in an inguinal sac, de Garengeot appendix in a femoral sac, Littre has a Meckel's diverticulum, Richter traps part of the wall.

You first swapped lateral and medial, then fixed it by following each sac's route: the indirect sac enters at the deep ring lateral to the vessels, the direct sac bulges through the posterior wall medial to them. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You pulled a ring or Cooper's ligament into Hesselbach's triangle, then rebuilt it from its three sides: inferior epigastric artery, lateral rectus border and inguinal ligament. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first read femoral hernia as the commonest in women, then separated a relative skew from a ranking: indirect inguinal still leads. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You started with an adult repair for a child, then tied the operation to the defect: a patent processus vaginalis with a normal posterior wall, so herniotomy alone. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first judged strangulation risk by size, then reasoned from the neck: the narrow neck at the deep ring grips the contents. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first answered with the inguinal ranking, then read the scope word: 'groin' includes femoral, which has the highest strangulation risk. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You reached for manual reduction first, then ordered the steps around bowel viability: resuscitate, then emergency surgery, no forceful taxis. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first chose the most advanced test, then used the ladder: no imaging for an evident hernia, ultrasound first for an occult one, MRI if ultrasound is inconclusive, CT for complications. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first applied one nerve to both approaches, then tied each to its field: ilioinguinal in open repair, lateral femoral cutaneous in laparoscopic repair. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first picked laparoscopic by default, then used the qualifiers: bilateral or recurrent favours it, and it needs general anaesthesia and expertise. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You started with the older Bassini key, then learned both: older PYQs expected Bassini, current practice is Lichtenstein mesh repair. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first reversed the occlusion test, then worked out which sac the finger blocks: an indirect sac is controlled, a direct sac still bulges medial to the finger. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You recalled fingertip rules by rote order rather than by anatomy. In Zieman's test the index finger sits over the deep ring (indirect), middle over the superficial ring (direct), ring finger over the saphenous opening (femoral). In the invagination test the tip suggests indirect and the pulp direct. You may have fixed it on the spot, but that does not show it holds. Meet it again on a fresh question: do its review card next.

You first gave the scrotal swelling to the direct hernia, then compared them side by side: the indirect sac follows the cord into the scrotum. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You swapped the two triangles, then separated them: doom holds the external iliac vessels, pain holds the nerves, with the gonadal vessels as the divider. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first put the conjoint tendon in the anterior wall, then compared the walls: the anterior wall is external oblique with internal oblique laterally; the posterior wall is transversalis fascia with the conjoint tendon medially. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You first gave direct hernia a congenital cause, then paired each with its own: indirect arises in a patent processus vaginalis, direct from posterior wall weakness. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.

You mixed the three operation terms, then ordered them by what is added to sac excision: herniotomy none, herniorrhaphy own tissue, hernioplasty mesh. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.
You first copied the inguinal position onto the femoral hernia, then traced its route below the inguinal ligament. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.
You swapped Amyand and de Garengeot, then anchored each to its site: Amyand inguinal, de Garengeot femoral. Under exam pressure this trap can return, so recheck it in the review card.
You tend to get a direction backwards, such as lateral versus medial, or what a test blocks. Predict the route first, then pick the answer.
You tend to skip qualifiers such as child versus adult, groin versus inguinal, open versus laparoscopic. Underline the qualifier before reading the options.
You tend to mismatch eponyms and associations: fingers, causes, triangles or appendix hernias. Practise them as paired recall with the discriminating feature.
You tend to mix up look-alike pairs, such as direct versus indirect pictures or the three operation terms. Next time, name the one feature that separates them before choosing.
You tapped Sure on more than one answer that turned out wrong. Those are the errors that survive revision, so review them first and treat a Sure tap as a prompt to check the qualifier.
You used no hints, so the traps you fell into were honest misses. Next time, a hint after a doubt is cheaper than a wrong first answer.
Do the review cards in the order listed: confident errors first, then gaps, then shaky areas. Retry the journey after a day, and tackle one gap per sitting.
